description: Square numbers, square roots and their patterns

lessons.title: What is a Square Number?
lessons.intro: A square number is what you get when you multiply a number by itself — like the area of a square!
explanation: We write it as 4 with a small 2: the exponent means 'times itself'.
lessons.rule: A square number = a number multiplied by itself.
lessons.tip: Picture a square grid: side x side.

steps.tip: Like the area of a 4x4 square.

lessons.title: Squares as Areas
lessons.intro: The area of a square equals its side multiplied by itself — a square number!
explanation: A tile with side 6 cm has area 6 x 6 = 36 sq cm.
That is why we call it 'squared'.
lessons.rule: Area of a square = side x side.

lessons.title: The First Squares
lessons.intro: Learning the first few square numbers by heart is very handy.
lessons.rule: Memorise squares of 1 to 10.
lessons.tip: Say them in order to spot the pattern.

lessons.title: Odd Number Pattern
lessons.intro: Square numbers grow by adding the next odd number each time — a lovely pattern.
explanation: The gaps are the odd numbers.
This shows why squares grow faster and faster.
lessons.rule: Each square = previous square + next odd number.

lessons.title: Squares in Problems
lessons.intro: Squares appear whenever something is arranged in a square grid.
explanation: A 9 x 9 garden has 81 square metres.
lessons.rule: Square-shaped layouts use square numbers.
lessons.tip: Count the side, then square it.

quiz.question: What is 4 squared?
What is 5 squared?
What is 7 squared?
What is 10 squared?
A square tile has a side of 6 cm. What is its area in square cm?
A square garden has a side of 9 m. What is its area in square metres?
What is 12 squared?
What is 15 squared?

lessons.title: Squares Beyond Ten
lessons.intro: Once you know squares to 10, you can learn the next ones up to 20.
explanation: These come up often in exams.
lessons.rule: Learn squares from 11 to 20 too.

steps.text: Multiply the teen number by itself.

lessons.title: Breaking Down Squares
lessons.intro: You can work out a square by splitting the number.
lessons.rule: Split a number to multiply it by itself.

lessons.title: Bigger Square Areas
lessons.intro: Large square rooms and plots use these bigger squares.
explanation: A 20 m square plot has area 400 sq m.
An 18 m square has area 324 sq m.
lessons.rule: Side squared gives even large square areas.

lessons.title: Spotting Squares to 400
lessons.intro: Knowing squares to 20 lets you recognise perfect squares up to 400.
explanation: Recognising them speeds up your work.
lessons.rule: Squares to 20 cover perfect squares up to 400.

lessons.title: Teen Square Master
lessons.intro: Practise all the teen squares until they are automatic.
explanation: Speed here pays off in exams.
lessons.rule: Master every square from 11 to 20.

quiz.question: What is 11 squared?
What is 13 squared?
What is 14 squared?
What is 16 squared?
A square room has a side of 20 m. What is its area in square metres?
A square board has a side of 18 cm. What is its area in square cm?
What is 17 squared?
What is 19 squared?

lessons.title: What is a Square Root?
lessons.intro: A square root undoes squaring — it asks 'what number times itself gives this?'
explanation: The square root of 36 is 6, because 6 x 6 = 36.
Square root is the opposite of squaring.
We use the radical sign for it.
lessons.rule: A square root is the number that was squared.
lessons.tip: Ask: what times itself gives this?

steps.text: Find the number that was squared.

lessons.title: Roots of Perfect Squares
lessons.intro: Perfect squares have whole-number square roots.
explanation: If you memorised the squares, you know the roots!
lessons.rule: Roots of perfect squares are whole numbers.
lessons.tip: Use your squares table in reverse.

lessons.title: Roots as Sides
lessons.intro: The square root of an area gives the side of a square.
explanation: A square field of 64 sq m has a side of 8 m.
Root of the area = the side.
Squaring the side gives back the area.
lessons.rule: Side of a square = square root of its area.

lessons.title: Using the Squares Table
lessons.intro: Finding roots is just reading your squares table backwards.
explanation: Know the square, know the root.
This is why learning squares pays off twice.
lessons.rule: Read squares backwards to get roots.

lessons.title: Root Master
lessons.intro: Practise roots of all perfect squares up to 225.
lessons.rule: Master roots of squares up to 225.
lessons.tip: Pair each square with its root.

quiz.question: What is the square root of 36?
What is the square root of 49?
What is the square root of 81?
What is the square root of 100?
A square field has an area of 64 square metres. What is the length of one side in metres?
A square of tiles covers 121 square cm. What is the length of one side in cm?
What is the square root of 144?
What is the square root of 225?

lessons.title: Perfect vs Not
lessons.intro: Not every number is a perfect square — some sit between two squares.
explanation: 25 is a perfect square; 24 is not.
lessons.rule: A perfect square is a whole number squared.
lessons.tip: Numbers ending in 2,3,7,8 are never perfect squares.

steps.text: Check if it is a whole number squared.

steps.tip: So 24 is not a perfect square.

lessons.title: Roots Between Whole Numbers
lessons.intro: The root of a non-perfect square lies between two whole numbers.
explanation: Square root of 20 is between 4 and 5 (since 16 and 25).
Find the squares just below and above.
The root sits between their roots.
lessons.rule: A root lies between the roots of the nearest squares.

lessons.title: Nearest Perfect Square
lessons.intro: We can find the perfect square closest to any number.
explanation: The nearest perfect square to 48 is 49.
Compare the squares on either side.
lessons.rule: Find the closest square above and below, then pick.

lessons.title: Squares in a Range
lessons.intro: You can list the perfect squares that fall in a given range.
explanation: Between 30 and 40, the perfect square is 36.
Check each square to see if it fits.
lessons.rule: List squares and see which land in the range.

lessons.title: Square Patterns Master
lessons.intro: Use square patterns to answer clever questions.
explanation: Difference of consecutive squares grows by odd numbers.
lessons.rule: Use sums and differences of squares in puzzles.
lessons.tip: Consecutive square gap = sum of the two roots.

quiz.question: Which is a perfect square, 24 or 25? Write it.
Is 50 a perfect square? Answer Yes or No.
The square root of 20 lies between 4 and which next whole number?
The square root of 90 lies between 9 and which next whole number?
What is the perfect square nearest to 48?
Which perfect square lies between 30 and 40?
What is the sum of the first three square numbers (1 + 4 + 9)?
What is 10 squared minus 9 squared?

lessons.title: Squares and Roots Together
lessons.intro: Now combine squaring and rooting in the same problem.
lessons.rule: Squaring and rooting are inverse operations.

lessons.title: Adding Squares
lessons.intro: Sometimes we add two squares together.
explanation: This pattern appears in geometry too.
lessons.rule: Square each number, then add the results.

lessons.title: Root of Bigger Squares
lessons.intro: Practise roots of larger perfect squares.
lessons.rule: Find roots of squares up to 400.

lessons.title: Adding Roots
lessons.intro: We can add two square roots of perfect squares.
explanation: Find each root first, then add.
lessons.rule: Find each root, then add them.

lessons.title: Square Master
lessons.intro: You can now handle any squares-and-roots challenge.
explanation: Confidence comes from knowing your tables.
lessons.rule: Combine squares and roots with full confidence.
